ra01.text: October twenty-eighteen. India's Supreme Court bans crackers made with barium salts, and joined crackers.

ra02.text: In Sivakasi, the town that makes most of India's fireworks, the factories go quiet. For about five months.

ra03.text: How does a town get this big, and this exposed to a single rule? The road starts a hundred years earlier, with a matchbox.

ra04.text: Follow the road. Try, but, so.

rb01.text: Find India on the globe. Now slide down to its far south, to Tamil Nadu.

rb02.text: Sivakasi sits in Virudhunagar district. It is hot, and it sits in the rain shadow of the hills to the west.

rb03.text: Farming here is hard, and families nearby need work. Villages around Sivakasi have plenty of labour, and little to do with it.

rb04.text: Three things to keep in mind. A match. A Bengal light, which is a match that burns in colour. And a firework.

rc01.text: Go back to nineteen twenty-two. Matches are made in Calcutta, today's Kolkata, or shipped in from abroad.

rc02.text: Two young men from Sivakasi make that trip. P. Ayya Nadar is about seventeen. A. Shanmuga Nadar is about nineteen.

rc03.text: They aren't going to learn fireworks. They're going to learn one thing: how to make a safety match.

rc04.text: They stay six to eight months, learning from a match-maker named Purna Chandra Roy.

rc05.text: In nineteen twenty-three they come home with German machines and open a match factory. The South-India Lucifer Match Industry.

rc06.text: But the German machines are costly to run in a small, remote town.

rc07.text: So they change the plan. They spread the work across the villages, to families with time to spare.

rc08.text: Families roll, fill and pack by hand, at home. The factory does only the chemical part.

rc09.text: It fits the mood of the time. Mahatma Gandhi is urging Indians to revive village industries.

rc10.text: Remember that choice. It builds the town. And a hundred years later, it is the hardest thing to change.

rd01.text: In nineteen twenty-six the two men part ways, and compete. Ayya Nadar's brand is a squirrel, Anil. Shanmuga Nadar's is a crow, Kaaka. A squirrel against a crow.

rd02.text: But a plain wooden match doesn't stand out. And each of the two rivals wants to.

rd03.text: To stand out, match-makers add something new: sticks that burn in colour. They're called Bengal lights. In Tamil, matthaappu.

rd04.text: Local histories treat the Bengal light as the stepping stone. A match that burns in colour is already close to a sparkler. And in nineteen thirty-eight, N. R. K. Rajarathina Nadar opens the town's first factory made only for fireworks.

rd04b.text: So matches led to coloured matches, and coloured matches led to fireworks. Not a tradition. A chain.

rd05.text: So far: a match, a hand network, a coloured flame. Each fixed the last problem.

re01.text: Every matchbox and every packet of crackers needs a bright paper label. In the nineteen thirties, those labels come from presses in Bombay, today's Mumbai.

re02.text: But waiting for labels from Bombay is slow. So in nineteen thirty-eight, K. S. A. Arunagiri Nadar sets up a printing press in Sivakasi itself.

re03.text: Picture a shop that sells most of its stock in one week, and keeps running out of paper cups from a far-off city. So the owner buys a printer. Then he notices it can print for the other eleven months too.

re04.text: That is Sivakasi's second trick. When the fireworks season ends, the presses keep running. Calendars. Diaries. Notebooks.

re05.text: Prime Minister Nehru is said to have called the town 'Kutty Japan', Little Japan, for making matches, fireworks and print on its own.

re06.text: A historian of the town, Rengaiah Murugan, put it simply: 'As a chain reaction, various allied industries started to mushroom.'

re07.text: So three links so far. The match. The coloured flame. The press. One more is coming, and it is not a machine. It is a war.

rf01.text: Now comes the moment that turns a good town into the national one. Nineteen-forty.

rf02.text: That year, the Explosives Rules arrive. To make fireworks, you now need a licence.

rf03.text: Then the Second World War cuts off the fireworks that used to come in from abroad.

rf04.text: The few licensed makers suddenly have the whole market. By nineteen forty-two, three firms hold licences: National, Standard and Kaliswari.

rf05.text: Three licensed factories in nineteen forty-two.

rf06.text: By nineteen eighty: a hundred and eighty-nine.

rf07.text: By two thousand and one: four hundred and fifty.

rf08.text: Today, the industry says, more than a thousand.

rf09.text: Worth about six thousand crore rupees a year. That is sixty billion rupees.

rf09b.text: Notice the pattern. Every step solved the last problem, and set up the next one.

rf10.text: That is the road up. Now back to the quiet sheds of twenty-eighteen.

rg01.text: But the ban hits barium, a core ingredient of the old recipe. For about five months, the town waits.

rg02.text: The industry's answer is the green cracker, developed by a government lab, CSIR-NEERI. Its versions are called SWAS, SAFAL and STAR.

rg03.text: Green doesn't mean pollution-free. The lab's own claim is about a third less particle pollution.

rg04.text: How? According to the lab, the mix releases water vapour and air as it burns, which helps the dust settle. Picture a tiny mist sprayer inside the shell.

rg04b.text: Delhi and its surroundings are roughly thirteen percent of national demand, industry associations estimate.

rg05.text: But even the fix has a catch. In October twenty twenty-five, the Court eases the Delhi ban for green crackers only, with QR codes, in fixed time slots. It comes just before Deepavali. A makers' leader said it comes too close to the festival, yet gives hope for future business.

rg06.text: So the fix is real, and it is partial. Less pollution, not none. And a market that opens in slots.

rh01.text: Now go back to the hands. By the industry's count, about three lakh people work in these factories. That is three hundred thousand. Many more work around them.

rh01b.text: Mixing, filling and threading fuses are still done mostly by hand.

rh01c.text: On paper, a small unit's licence limits how many people may work inside. Reports say twelve.

rh02.text: Reports describe sheds sub-let to contractors, and crowded verandahs. A gap between the licence and the workplace.

rh03.text: On the nineteenth of April, twenty twenty-six, an explosion at a factory near Sivakasi killed twenty-five workers.

rh04.text: A worker, K. Rajkumar, told The Hindu that with a biometric attendance system, identifying the dead would not have been so hard.

rh05.text: The road began with a choice to spread the work across many hands. It built the town. Now the same choice asks for a new safety answer.

rj00.text: In May twenty twenty-five, the makers' association applied for a GI tag for Sivakasi fireworks. It's a legal label of origin. Their lawyer says it would help curb duplicates.

rj01.text: Try, but, so. A match, then hands. A flame, then a press. A war, then a market. A ban, then a green recipe.

rj02.text: In twenty-eighteen the lights went out in Sivakasi. The town did not make fireworks for centuries. It learned to make them, one fix at a time.

rj03.text: Its next fix is the hardest: to keep the people who light the sky safe.
